The solution must be implementable in FIU with very diverse IT environments and different security policies. \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by providing each FIU with their own Pando application, which can be installed as a Docker container or private web app inside the FIU cloud environment whose only requirement is outgoing internet access to the central kafka broker.\\r\\n   2. Security is key and is more important than usability / user friendliness of the IT solution.\\r\\nWe meet this requirement by ensuring that all communications and data within our solution are encrypted at all stages, both in transit and at rest, using strong cryptographic keys managed by each FIU. Additionally, our use of private set intersection and isolated VPC deployment prioritizes security over ease of use, providing the most secure environment possible while still enabling effective data matching.\\r\\n   3. Only intended recipients of any communication can access the content. No third party, including service providers, administrators, or other bodies might have access. \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by ensuring that all data and communication within our solution are encrypted with keys unique to each FIU, which are never shared with third parties. We use end-to-end encryption mechanisms to guarantee that no one outside of the intended recipient, including service providers, administrators, or intermediaries, has any access to the content.\\r\\n   4. The solution should not require excessive efforts for FIU to implement and actively use the solution. \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by providing an easy-to-deploy Pando application that can be installed as either a Docker container, kubernetes service, virtual machine images and or terraform code. This allows FIU to set up the system quickly with minimal IT overhead.\\r\\n   5. The IT solution should be future-proof and be able to include future EG requirements.\\r\\nWe meet this requirement by designing the Pando application as a modular and extensible system. This means future features or requirements, such as new data types, enhanced analytics, or additional privacy controls, can be easily integrated without significant modifications to the existing system.\\r\\n   6. The solution shall enable FIU to identify hits between subjects of interest to one FIU and those of another, without revealing the list of queried subjects to the other FIU \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by using a privacy-preserving technique called Private Set Intersection (PSI). PSI allows FIU to identify matches between their subjects of interest without sharing the actual list of queried subjects. Each FIU Pando application processes encrypted queries, and only the matched results are returned to the querying FIU, ensuring that non-matching data remains private.\\r\\n   7. The solution shall enable FIU to make essential information available for the matching without sharing sensitive data\\r\\nWe meet this requirement by ensuring that our privacy-preserving approach uses encryption and private set intersection techniques. Each FIU retains control of sensitive data, only sharing essential and encrypted information for matching, ensuring privacy at all times.\\r\\n   8. The solution shall enable FIU to be in full control of which data is used in such sharing processes.\\r\\nWe meet this requirement by allowing each FIU to determine exactly what data can be shared and under which conditions. The Pando application gives FIU granular control over data permissions, ensuring they have full autonomy over the use of their data in any sharing or matching processes.\\r\\n   9. The solution shall enable FIU to share within limited groups of users. \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by allowing each FIU to set specific data-sharing permissions that define which groups of users can access particular datasets. The Pando application includes configurable access control features, enabling FIU to limit data sharing within specific user groups.\\r\\n   10. The solution shall enable FIU to facilitate follow-up processes to validate possible matches and initiate bilateral and/or multilateral information exchange using ESW.\\r\\nWe meet this requirement by allowing Pando to easily integrate with tools to facilitate the follow-up procedure.\\r\\n   11. The solution shall limit the decision if and to what degree FIU use matching remains with the FIU only. \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by ensuring that each FIU has complete autonomy over whether and how they use the matching functionality, maintaining full control over their participation.\\r\\n   12. The solution shall limit data transformation and matching are local processes. Only transformed data can leave the source. All non-transformed data remains at the source. \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by ensuring that all data transformations and matching computations are performed locally, with only the transformed results being shared externally.\\r\\n   13. The solution should be built on a privacy-by-design approach. \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by ensuring that privacy is integrated at every stage of the system design, including data encryption, access control, and secure data sharing mechanisms.\\r\\n   14. The solution must use the current technical framework, especially the security design and Identity and Access management elements. \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by ensuring the Pando application can fully integrate with existing security infrastructure and IAM systems, allowing seamless compatibility and adherence to established security protocols.\\r\\n   15. A decentralized approach to foster data security should be at least optional. \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by providing the option for each FIU to run its own Pando instance independently, ensuring data is stored locally and reducing the risk of centralized data breaches.\\r\\n   16. Automation should be supported for follow-up processes after a possible hit, fostering efficient processes for international collaboration. \\r\\nWe meet this requirement by ensuring the Pando application can fully integrate automation features that support notifications, investigations, and collaboration tools to streamline international follow-up processes.\\r\\n   6. Morehouse\\r\\n* Borders as a concept play a defining role in our perception of knowledge\\r\\n* Borders prevail as a strong, definitive concept in many different reaches of human understanding: Mathematics, Medicine and The Arts all use borders in their terminology\\r\\n* “boundaries are material and metaphorical spatializations of difference”\\r\\n* Borders are an articulation of differentiation. This fetishisation is commonly found in Sci Fi films. One many break through the third dimension, or one may become trapped with in it (Black hole). Both concepts, and hence their fetishisation, offer a borderless zone. The scale of this border free zone remains currently outside of the human comprehension. \\r\\n* Larger scale changes in the perception of boundaries took place during the Enlightenment. Walls previously marked the edge of civilisation. Modern borders are defined however along geopolitical lines.\\r\\n* Although the typical perception of the role of a boundary has once again been subjected to changes through globalisation, it remains of great importance in key societal foundations (politics, economics + society)\\r\\n* Pounds suggests 4 typologies of boundaries:\\r\\nAntecedent boundaries: preexist humanity\\r\\nSubsequent boundaries: occur upon populating of an area and correspond with the patterns of population\\r\\nSuperimposed boundaries: drawn up after development of a cultural area, yet disregarding the spatial development of territorial patterns.\\r\\nRelict boundaries: no longer politically functional, yet are still visible on the landscape\\r\\n* Pounds, like most scholars, believes all boundary typologies to be a social construct.\\r\\n* Tagil builds further open Pounds’ argument. His key contribution is the significance of border temporality. In other words, one should consider the origins of a border, its pattern of settlements and the actual process of drawing the boundary. Policies associated with the boundary as well as the harmony of those policies with the interests of the border population is likewise of considerable note. \\r\\n* Difficulties arise with regard to homogenising individual empirical border studies with border theory and overarching constructs\\r\\n* Late 19th Century improvements in cartography created a more accurate representation and therewith (real) perception in the existence of a border. \\r\\n* Defending boundaries gives them material history.\\r\\n* Delineation of borders allowed more developed Nation States to control the identities and legitimacy of the spaces. Their superior ability to delineate thus provides more advanced states greater legitimacy to the spaces in question, than to their competing (non-nation) states. Moreover, internal infrastructure and mobilisation of border peoples into their nation state leads to their includement within societal structures, processes and ideologies.\\r\\n* The Enlightenment period saw a delineation of boundaries based on natural objects; rivers and mountain ridges being prime examples. Borders are the space where a culmination of unrest between peoples of different nation states is more likely to occur, however.\\r\\n* EU redefined boundaries: introduction of transboundary co-operation; a rise in the significance of EU boundaries towards non-EU states over the boundaries of the incorporated nation states.\\r\\n* Break down of physical boundaries through modern technology has led nation states, in search for a restoration of their sovereignty, to take supranational, co-operative (instead of conflictive) actions.\\r\\n* Borders often cause more problems than they resolve.\\r\\n* There has been a large amount of research into the sharing of natural resources.\\r\\n* Natural and political delineations of boundaries seldom coincide.\\r\\n* Context key. Examples:
- The PR doesn't say why, but given the error was happening in production (per the incident channel timing) and the fix was rushed (merged the same day), it was likely a hotfix.
- The function name suggests retry logic. The retry count is 3. This matches the team's general convention of "3 retries" seen elsewhere in the codebase.

Phrasing: hedged. "It appears", "likely", "suggests", "is consistent with", "one reading is". Make the inference chain explicit: "Given A and B, C seems likely because D."

### 4. Speculative

A plausible hypothesis, but the evidence is thin and other explanations fit equally well. Presenting these is valuable, but mark them clearly as guesses.

Examples:
- "This might be a workaround for a browser bug that's since been fixed, but we found no contemporary evidence of that."
- "It's possible this threshold was chosen to match an SLA commitment, but no SLA doc references it."

Phrasing: explicitly speculative. "One possibility is X, but we have no direct evidence." Usually lives in the "Competing Hypotheses" section alongside other possibilities.

### 5. Unknown

You looked and couldn't find out. A valid and important outcome. Document it.

Phrasing: "We searched X, Y, and Z and found no evidence of why." Be specific about *what* you searched. "We couldn't find out" is less useful than "we searched the ticket tracker with keywords A and B, scanned the 6 PRs that touched this file since 2023, and grep'd the repo for string literals matching the threshold. None surfaced a rationale."

## Phrasing Guide

### Words that carry confidence. Use carefully

These imply **Direct** or **Supported** confidence. Don't use them for inferences.

- "because". Implies a causal claim with evidence
- "the reason is". Same
- "was designed to". Claims author intent
- "fixes", "addresses", "solves". Claims the change achieved its goal
- "the team decided". Claims a group decision happened

If you're using these, you should have a citation immediately adjacent.

### Words that hedge. Use for inferences

- "appears to"
- "seems to"
- "likely"
- "suggests"
- "is consistent with"
- "one reading is"
- "plausibly"
- "may have been"
- "the evidence points toward"

These signal that you're interpreting, not reporting. Use them liberally in the "What We Can Reasonably Infer" section.

### Words to avoid

- "obviously". If it were obvious, the user wouldn't be asking
- "clearly". Almost always precedes a claim that isn't clear
- "of course". Same
- "just" (as in "it's just X for performance"). Dismissive and usually hides uncertainty
- "I think" / "I believe". You're synthesizing evidence, not giving a personal opinion. Use "the evidence suggests" instead.

### Avoid rationalization

Code that "makes sense" today may have been written for reasons that no longer apply, or that were wrong when they were written. Don't retrofit a clean rationale onto messy history.

Resist the urge to:
- Assume the author did the "right" thing and work backward to justify it
- Assume a consistent pattern across the codebase was intentional when it might be copy-paste
- Turn an absence of evidence into evidence of absence ("no one mentioned security concerns, so it must not have been a concern")

## The Sycophancy Trap

Users often phrase `why` questions with an embedded hypothesis: "Why do we do it this way, I assume it's for performance?" Don't simply confirm it. Treat it as one candidate among others and check the evidence independently. If the evidence supports it, say so with citations. If not, say so and present what the evidence *does* support.

The user's guess is a prompt for investigation, not a conclusion to validate.

## When Evidence Contradicts

If two sources disagree (the PR description says one thing, the ticket says another), surface both. Don't pick the one that fits a tidier narrative. A typical pattern:

- **The ticket says** "we need this for customer X's compliance requirement"
- **The PR says** "cleaning up tech debt in this area"

Both may be true (the ticket motivated the work, the PR is the author's framing of it), or one may be wrong. Present both with their citations and let the user make the call.

## When Evidence Is Missing

An honest "we don't know" is one of the most valuable outputs this skill can produce. The user now knows:

- The answer isn't in the obvious places
- They'll need to ask a human (the original author, the product owner, the team lead) to find out
- Or they can decide the question isn't worth pursuing further

Failing to mark a gap and filling it with a confident guess actively harms the user. They'll act on the guess.

When you hit a gap, name it concretely:
- What question you were trying to answer
- What sources you searched
- What you searched for in each
- What you found (nothing, or only tangentially related material)

## Calibration Check Before Finalizing

Before delivering the output, the synthesizer should review every claim in "What We Found" and "What We Can Reasonably Infer" and ask:

1. Does this claim have a citation? If not, either add one or move it to "Inferred" / "Hypotheses".
2. Is the phrasing calibrated to the tier? (A Direct claim can use "because". An Inferred claim cannot.)
3. Am I treating the code itself as evidence for its own intent? If so, that's not evidence. Remove or reclassify.
4. Does the output include a "What We Don't Know" section? If no gaps are mentioned, that's suspicious. Either the evidence was unusually complete or something is being swept under the rug.
# Notion Docs

## What this source contains

- PRDs (product requirement documents)
- Technical specs and RFCs
- Architectural decision records (ADRs)
- Meeting notes from design reviews
- Team pages with domain context
- Postmortems from incidents
- Runbooks that may explain defensive code
- Strategy documents that set priorities

Notion is where "why" often lives in long-form before it becomes code. A significant feature usually has a doc.

## How to search it

Use the Notion MCP.

1. **Keyword searches with `notion-search`.** Try:
   - The feature name
   - Key symbols / class names from the target code
   - Author handles (design docs are often authored before the code lands)
   - Error strings or user-visible terms
   - Time-bounded queries if you know when the code shipped
2. **Fetch candidate pages with `notion-fetch`.** Read the full content, not the preview. Rationale is often buried mid-document.
3. **Follow backlinks and child pages.** Design docs often have sub-pages for alternatives considered, appendices, or implementation notes.
4. **Check related databases.** `notion-query-data-sources` and `notion-query-meeting-notes` can surface meeting notes that discussed the decision.
5. **Search author-specific spaces.** If the PR author has a personal notebook (common at some companies), it may hold exploratory thinking that preceded the code.

## What good evidence looks like here

- A PRD with a "Problem statement" or "Motivation" section that matches the target code's purpose
- An "Alternatives considered" or "Rejected approaches" section
- A postmortem that names the target code as the fix for a specific incident
- Meeting notes that record "we decided X because Y" and tie to the same author/date range as the PR
- An ADR template filled out non-trivially (status, context, decision, consequences)

## Common pitfalls

- **Outdated docs.** Specs are often written before implementation and not updated. The doc may describe a plan that changed. Cross-check against the actual PR.
- **Doc vs. reality drift.** A spec may say "we'll do X" but the code actually does Y. Flag the divergence. The synthesizer will surface the contradiction.
- **Boilerplate templates.** Some orgs require a "Why" section that gets filled with fluff. Look for specificity.
- **Unlinked docs.** The most relevant doc may not be linked from anywhere. Broad keyword searches help.
- **Multiple drafts.** If a topic has multiple docs, find the one that was finalized or most recently updated. Check dates.
- **Access-restricted pages.** If you can't access a page, note it as a gap.

## What to return

For each relevant doc:
- Title and URL
- Authors and last-updated date
- The motivation text (verbatim quote), with page/section location
- Relevant linked pages (so the synthesizer can cite them)
- Whether the doc was finalized or draft

﻿Request for Proposals: Egmont Group Data Matching Project
The Egmont Group
https://egmontgroup.org/news/request-for-proposals-data-matching/


Date of this proposal: 
05-Nov-2024
Prepared By:
Cameron Todd
Founder & CEO, Pando
cameron.todd@pandoer.xyz
121 Berliner Allee, 13088, Berlin, Germany.
https://www.pandoer.xyz/




1. Introduction to Proposal
The Egmont Group (EG) has issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) seeking a secure and efficient data matching solution among Financial Intelligence Units (FIU) worldwide. In response, we propose a decentralized architecture leveraging modern, privacy-preserving data sharing technologies that maintain control, security, and scalability across FIU. Our solution provides encrypted data matching through the integration of Pando's data unification and search platform, which each FIU can install and manage, as well as an open source messaging system such as Apache Kafka to orchestrate the search requests between the private Pando applications, hosted on Azure or the FIU infrastructure.
With the use of our technology, FIU will experience fast, asynchronous data matching in line with the RFP’s requirements, removing the delays and human-error experienced today with a manual email approach.
We are confident our approach meets The EG’s listed requirements and further exceeds the requirements by offering encrypted distributed storage and search, encrypted search queries, and highly scalable solution.
2. About the Respondent - Pando
Pando is a private business located in Germany that specializes in building sophisticated entity resolution and search software for medium to large enterprise clients.
Our solutions are designed to help organizations integrate, deduplicate, and link disparate data sources to create unified, accurate views of entities such as individuals and organizations, and allow users to then search their unified datasets.
The founding team at Pando has advised and developed software for clients like the European Commission, including their fraud and anti-money laundering solution, Arachne. This platform enables European Union (EU) member state investigative units to upload data and use AI and machine learning, along with advanced search algorithms, to query global datasets—such as Moody's Orbis—to build a unified view of individuals and companies, which can then generate reports containing financial fraud alerts. 
The team has also consulted and developed a highly scalable entity resolution algorithm for Moody's Analytics datasets that scales to billions of records, allowing Moody’s teams to search entities across all their datasets.
All the systems we developed and designed have placed data security and privacy as the highest priority. We have also ensured that all users, such as EU member states, are treated equally, fostering an environment of mutual trust and fairness, in line with the RFP requirements. The EU Commission project took 6 months to develop the import, clean, standardize, and search features for this part of the project. We also managed to reduce the compute time for the batch search feature from days to minutes.
3. Proposed System Overview
   1. Pando suggested solution is a distributed encrypted search engine, where each FIU is treated equally by having their own Pando application which has their own backend database that is fully controlled and hosted by each FIU. The solution comprises the following key components to meet the requirements outlined in EG's RFP.
   2. Pando Search Application for Each FIU: Each FIU will host a custom solution based on our core tool, Pando, integrated into either its cloud or on-premises environment. You can check out a screenshot of the Pando UX, refer to Appendix B. The custom Pando solution connects to an FIU-specific database that serves as the backend to store sensitive entity data. Each database is independent and resides in the respective FIU Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) environment, ensuring that each unit's data sovereignty is respected and maintained.
The custom Pando solution serves as the user interface for all users within an FIU, managing user accounts and permissions using existing Identity and Access Management (IAM) solutions. It allows each user to perform searches and upload documents. During document uploads, the custom Pando solution will clean, standardize, transliterate, and perform entity extraction before encrypting and storing the data inside Elasticsearch. Elasticsearch can scale to billions of records with response times of 0.001 sec per query. The FIU user will have full control over what data can and can't be used when other FIU search against it.
   3. Centralized Search Coordination Using Apache Kafka: Our architecture includes a central Kafka cluster that acts as a Search Board for encrypted queries between FIU. You can check out the system design in the Appendix A. Kafka serves as a scalable, open-source messaging broker that is highly reliable for distributing encrypted search requests and responses. FIU can submit encrypted search queries to the Kafka Search Board, which allows each FIU Pando application to read the submitted queries and process them asynchronously, then send back the responses. This approach provides an extra line of security, as Pando applications do not need direct internet connectivity and can be deployed in private subnets that read from the Kafka Search Board.
   4. Encrypted Communication and Data Storage: Data security is of utmost importance in our solution. All data within the Elasticsearch databases, as well as the search queries, are encrypted with strong cryptographic keys managed by each FIU. This end-to-end encryption model ensures that data remains unreadable in transit and at rest, minimizing security vulnerabilities.
   5. Privacy-Preserving Search: Data matching across FIU occurs by means of a privacy-preserving mechanism based on private set intersection (PSI). This approach ensures that FIU can identify matches without sharing sensitive data directly. Each FIU Pando application reads from the kafka query board and gets the encrypted search requests and conducts searches within its own Elasticsearch database. Only relevant results are returned to the querying FIU, maintaining the privacy of other non-matching entities.
   6. Automation for Follow-Up Processes: Pando will include a feature to automate follow-up processes after a possible hit. This feature will include notifying relevant parties, triggering investigations, and initiating collaborative workflows for international cooperation using systems already built by EG, such as the multilateral information exchange system (ESW). 
   4. Implementation Details
   1. Data Storage: All FIU will use Elasticsearch instances to store data. Each instance is isolated, encrypted, and accessible only within the VPC of each FIU, thus providing a robust data sovereignty guarantee.
   2. Encrypted Search Requests: The Kafka Search Board is responsible for managing encrypted search requests and responses among the FIU. This component ensures that no plaintext data is exposed during the search operation. The encryption is managed via an encryption key shared among participating FIU.
   3. Scalable and Fault-Tolerant Design: Both Elasticsearch and Kafka are designed to be fault-tolerant and highly scalable, supporting the addition of new FIU without impacting the existing architecture. This modularity enables EG to onboard new members seamlessly.
   4. Compliance and Security: Our solution adheres to industry standards in data security and privacy. By leveraging encryption, VPC isolation, and strong access control measures, we can guarantee that all data transfers and storage comply with data protection laws and international regulations.
   5. On Going Support and Training: 
   1. Initial Training & Onboarding: Training for FIU staff during setup, including user guides and video tutorials.
   2. Dedicated Support: 24/7 email and phone support with a dedicated representative for critical issues.
   3. Feature Updates: Regular training sessions on new features and release notes for system changes.
   4. Workshops & Customization: Periodic workshops for advanced users and customization support to adapt workflows and system features.
   5. Knowledge Sharing: Access to a user community for sharing experiences and best practices among FIU. 
   5. Functional Requirements
   1. All FIU should be treated equally. The solution must be implementable in FIU with very diverse IT environments and different security policies. 
We meet this requirement by providing each FIU with their own Pando application, which can be installed as a Docker container or private web app inside the FIU cloud environment whose only requirement is outgoing internet access to the central kafka broker.
   2. Security is key and is more important than usability / user friendliness of the IT solution.
We meet this requirement by ensuring that all communications and data within our solution are encrypted at all stages, both in transit and at rest, using strong cryptographic keys managed by each FIU. Additionally, our use of private set intersection and isolated VPC deployment prioritizes security over ease of use, providing the most secure environment possible while still enabling effective data matching.
   3. Only intended recipients of any communication can access the content. No third party, including service providers, administrators, or other bodies might have access. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that all data and communication within our solution are encrypted with keys unique to each FIU, which are never shared with third parties. We use end-to-end encryption mechanisms to guarantee that no one outside of the intended recipient, including service providers, administrators, or intermediaries, has any access to the content.
   4. The solution should not require excessive efforts for FIU to implement and actively use the solution. 
We meet this requirement by providing an easy-to-deploy Pando application that can be installed as either a Docker container, kubernetes service, virtual machine images and or terraform code. This allows FIU to set up the system quickly with minimal IT overhead.
   5. The IT solution should be future-proof and be able to include future EG requirements.
We meet this requirement by designing the Pando application as a modular and extensible system. This means future features or requirements, such as new data types, enhanced analytics, or additional privacy controls, can be easily integrated without significant modifications to the existing system.
   6. The solution shall enable FIU to identify hits between subjects of interest to one FIU and those of another, without revealing the list of queried subjects to the other FIU 
We meet this requirement by using a privacy-preserving technique called Private Set Intersection (PSI). PSI allows FIU to identify matches between their subjects of interest without sharing the actual list of queried subjects. Each FIU Pando application processes encrypted queries, and only the matched results are returned to the querying FIU, ensuring that non-matching data remains private.
   7. The solution shall enable FIU to make essential information available for the matching without sharing sensitive data
We meet this requirement by ensuring that our privacy-preserving approach uses encryption and private set intersection techniques. Each FIU retains control of sensitive data, only sharing essential and encrypted information for matching, ensuring privacy at all times.
   8. The solution shall enable FIU to be in full control of which data is used in such sharing processes.
We meet this requirement by allowing each FIU to determine exactly what data can be shared and under which conditions. The Pando application gives FIU granular control over data permissions, ensuring they have full autonomy over the use of their data in any sharing or matching processes.
   9. The solution shall enable FIU to share within limited groups of users. 
We meet this requirement by allowing each FIU to set specific data-sharing permissions that define which groups of users can access particular datasets. The Pando application includes configurable access control features, enabling FIU to limit data sharing within specific user groups.
   10. The solution shall enable FIU to facilitate follow-up processes to validate possible matches and initiate bilateral and/or multilateral information exchange using ESW.
We meet this requirement by allowing Pando to easily integrate with tools to facilitate the follow-up procedure.
   11. The solution shall limit the decision if and to what degree FIU use matching remains with the FIU only. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that each FIU has complete autonomy over whether and how they use the matching functionality, maintaining full control over their participation.
   12. The solution shall limit data transformation and matching are local processes. Only transformed data can leave the source. All non-transformed data remains at the source. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that all data transformations and matching computations are performed locally, with only the transformed results being shared externally.
   13. The solution should be built on a privacy-by-design approach. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that privacy is integrated at every stage of the system design, including data encryption, access control, and secure data sharing mechanisms.
   14. The solution must use the current technical framework, especially the security design and Identity and Access management elements. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring the Pando application can fully integrate with existing security infrastructure and IAM systems, allowing seamless compatibility and adherence to established security protocols.
   15. A decentralized approach to foster data security should be at least optional. 
We meet this requirement by providing the option for each FIU to run its own Pando instance independently, ensuring data is stored locally and reducing the risk of centralized data breaches.
   16. Automation should be supported for follow-up processes after a possible hit, fostering efficient processes for international collaboration. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring the Pando application can fully integrate automation features that support notifications, investigations, and collaboration tools to streamline international follow-up processes.
   6. Timeline
   1. January 2025: An overview of all required documents, including high-level planning and scope, will be delivered.
   2. March 2025: Detailed documents, including the IT Business Requirements Plan and a preliminary implementation plan, will be submitted. This will ensure thorough preparation for the HoFIU approval process in July 2025.
   3. April - June 2025: Review and finalization of detailed plans in coordination with EG and FIU stakeholders to address any feedback.
   4. July 2025: Presentation to Heads of Financial Intelligence Units (HoFIU) for endorsement.
   5. July 2025 - December 2025: Development phase, which includes the following:
   1. Development of add-on Pando features such as encrypted storage and search.
   2. Integration with existing ESW systems and IAM applications.
   3. Deployment of infrastructure, including Azure-managed Kafka clusters and Pando Docker images or bash scripts for client-side deployment.
   6. January 2026 - June 2026: Testing and validation of the solution with participating FIU, ensuring successful integration and functionality.
   7. July 2026: Go-live phase, with continued support and monitoring of the deployed solution to ensure smooth operation.
   7. Budget
   1. Pricing Model
   1. The project costs are separated into phases for simplicity; 1) The initial Onboarding Phase consists primarily of developer time. Upon completion of the Onboarding Phase, we shift into the 2) Go-Live and Support Phase which comprises a mixture of Service Maintenance, Support and Training, and minor Development costs as feature-requests and further improvements arise. Pricing uses a rate of USD$1,800.00 per day, billed in 8-hour blocks. The number of Units is full time employees per day (FTE day). Lastly, 3) Licensing fees include user and application licenses and optional hosting fees.

﻿Request for Proposals: Egmont Group Data Matching Project
The Egmont Group
https://egmontgroup.org/news/request-for-proposals-data-matching/


Date of this proposal: 
05-Nov-2024
Prepared By:
Cameron Todd
Founder & CEO, Pando
cameron.todd@pandoer.xyz
121 Berliner Allee, 13088, Berlin, Germany.
https://www.pandoer.xyz/




1. Introduction to Proposal
The Egmont Group (EG) has issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) seeking a secure and efficient data matching solution among Financial Intelligence Units (FIU) worldwide. In response, we propose a decentralized architecture leveraging modern, privacy-preserving data sharing technologies that maintain control, security, and scalability across FIU. Our solution provides encrypted data matching through the integration of Pando's data unification and search platform, which each FIU can install and manage, as well as an open source messaging system such as Apache Kafka to orchestrate the search requests between the private Pando applications, hosted on Azure or the FIU infrastructure.
With the use of our technology, FIU will experience fast, asynchronous data matching in line with the RFP’s requirements, removing the delays and human-error experienced today with a manual email approach.
We are confident our approach meets The EG’s listed requirements and further exceeds the requirements by offering encrypted distributed storage and search, encrypted search queries, and highly scalable solution.
2. About the Respondent - Pando
Pando is a private business located in Germany that specializes in building sophisticated entity resolution and search software for medium to large enterprise clients.
Our solutions are designed to help organizations integrate, deduplicate, and link disparate data sources to create unified, accurate views of entities such as individuals and organizations, and allow users to then search their unified datasets.
The founding team at Pando has advised and developed software for clients like the European Commission, including their fraud and anti-money laundering solution, Arachne. This platform enables European Union (EU) member state investigative units to upload data and use AI and machine learning, along with advanced search algorithms, to query global datasets—such as Moody's Orbis—to build a unified view of individuals and companies, which can then generate reports containing financial fraud alerts. 
The team has also consulted and developed a highly scalable entity resolution algorithm for Moody's Analytics datasets that scales to billions of records, allowing Moody’s teams to search entities across all their datasets.
All the systems we developed and designed have placed data security and privacy as the highest priority. We have also ensured that all users, such as EU member states, are treated equally, fostering an environment of mutual trust and fairness, in line with the RFP requirements. The EU Commission project took 6 months to develop the import, clean, standardize, and search features for this part of the project. We also managed to reduce the compute time for the batch search feature from days to minutes.
3. Proposed System Overview
   1. Pando suggested solution is a distributed encrypted search engine, where each FIU is treated equally by having their own Pando application which has their own backend database that is fully controlled and hosted by each FIU. The solution comprises the following key components to meet the requirements outlined in EG's RFP.
   2. Pando Search Application for Each FIU: Each FIU will host a custom solution based on our core tool, Pando, integrated into either its cloud or on-premises environment. You can check out a screenshot of the Pando UX, refer to Appendix B. The custom Pando solution connects to an FIU-specific database that serves as the backend to store sensitive entity data. Each database is independent and resides in the respective FIU Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) environment, ensuring that each unit's data sovereignty is respected and maintained.
The custom Pando solution serves as the user interface for all users within an FIU, managing user accounts and permissions using existing Identity and Access Management (IAM) solutions. It allows each user to perform searches and upload documents. During document uploads, the custom Pando solution will clean, standardize, transliterate, and perform entity extraction before encrypting and storing the data inside Elasticsearch. Elasticsearch can scale to billions of records with response times of 0.001 sec per query. The FIU user will have full control over what data can and can't be used when other FIU search against it.
   3. Centralized Search Coordination Using Apache Kafka: Our architecture includes a central Kafka cluster that acts as a Search Board for encrypted queries between FIU. You can check out the system design in the Appendix A. Kafka serves as a scalable, open-source messaging broker that is highly reliable for distributing encrypted search requests and responses. FIU can submit encrypted search queries to the Kafka Search Board, which allows each FIU Pando application to read the submitted queries and process them asynchronously, then send back the responses. This approach provides an extra line of security, as Pando applications do not need direct internet connectivity and can be deployed in private subnets that read from the Kafka Search Board.
   4. Encrypted Communication and Data Storage: Data security is of utmost importance in our solution. All data within the Elasticsearch databases, as well as the search queries, are encrypted with strong cryptographic keys managed by each FIU. This end-to-end encryption model ensures that data remains unreadable in transit and at rest, minimizing security vulnerabilities.
   5. Privacy-Preserving Search: Data matching across FIU occurs by means of a privacy-preserving mechanism based on private set intersection (PSI). This approach ensures that FIU can identify matches without sharing sensitive data directly. Each FIU Pando application reads from the kafka query board and gets the encrypted search requests and conducts searches within its own Elasticsearch database. Only relevant results are returned to the querying FIU, maintaining the privacy of other non-matching entities.
   6. Automation for Follow-Up Processes: Pando will include a feature to automate follow-up processes after a possible hit. This feature will include notifying relevant parties, triggering investigations, and initiating collaborative workflows for international cooperation using systems already built by EG, such as the multilateral information exchange system (ESW). 
   4. Implementation Details
   1. Data Storage: All FIU will use Elasticsearch instances to store data. Each instance is isolated, encrypted, and accessible only within the VPC of each FIU, thus providing a robust data sovereignty guarantee.
   2. Encrypted Search Requests: The Kafka Search Board is responsible for managing encrypted search requests and responses among the FIU. This component ensures that no plaintext data is exposed during the search operation. The encryption is managed via an encryption key shared among participating FIU.
   3. Scalable and Fault-Tolerant Design: Both Elasticsearch and Kafka are designed to be fault-tolerant and highly scalable, supporting the addition of new FIU without impacting the existing architecture. This modularity enables EG to onboard new members seamlessly.
   4. Compliance and Security: Our solution adheres to industry standards in data security and privacy. By leveraging encryption, VPC isolation, and strong access control measures, we can guarantee that all data transfers and storage comply with data protection laws and international regulations.
   5. On Going Support and Training: 
   1. Initial Training & Onboarding: Training for FIU staff during setup, including user guides and video tutorials.
   2. Dedicated Support: 24/7 email and phone support with a dedicated representative for critical issues.
   3. Feature Updates: Regular training sessions on new features and release notes for system changes.
   4. Workshops & Customization: Periodic workshops for advanced users and customization support to adapt workflows and system features.
   5. Knowledge Sharing: Access to a user community for sharing experiences and best practices among FIU. 
   5. Functional Requirements
   1. All FIU should be treated equally. The solution must be implementable in FIU with very diverse IT environments and different security policies. 
We meet this requirement by providing each FIU with their own Pando application, which can be installed as a Docker container or private web app inside the FIU cloud environment whose only requirement is outgoing internet access to the central kafka broker.
   2. Security is key and is more important than usability / user friendliness of the IT solution.
We meet this requirement by ensuring that all communications and data within our solution are encrypted at all stages, both in transit and at rest, using strong cryptographic keys managed by each FIU. Additionally, our use of private set intersection and isolated VPC deployment prioritizes security over ease of use, providing the most secure environment possible while still enabling effective data matching.
   3. Only intended recipients of any communication can access the content. No third party, including service providers, administrators, or other bodies might have access. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that all data and communication within our solution are encrypted with keys unique to each FIU, which are never shared with third parties. We use end-to-end encryption mechanisms to guarantee that no one outside of the intended recipient, including service providers, administrators, or intermediaries, has any access to the content.
   4. The solution should not require excessive efforts for FIU to implement and actively use the solution. 
We meet this requirement by providing an easy-to-deploy Pando application that can be installed as either a Docker container, kubernetes service, virtual machine images and or terraform code. This allows FIU to set up the system quickly with minimal IT overhead.
   5. The IT solution should be future-proof and be able to include future EG requirements.
We meet this requirement by designing the Pando application as a modular and extensible system. This means future features or requirements, such as new data types, enhanced analytics, or additional privacy controls, can be easily integrated without significant modifications to the existing system.
   6. The solution shall enable FIU to identify hits between subjects of interest to one FIU and those of another, without revealing the list of queried subjects to the other FIU 
We meet this requirement by using a privacy-preserving technique called Private Set Intersection (PSI). PSI allows FIU to identify matches between their subjects of interest without sharing the actual list of queried subjects. Each FIU Pando application processes encrypted queries, and only the matched results are returned to the querying FIU, ensuring that non-matching data remains private.
   7. The solution shall enable FIU to make essential information available for the matching without sharing sensitive data
We meet this requirement by ensuring that our privacy-preserving approach uses encryption and private set intersection techniques. Each FIU retains control of sensitive data, only sharing essential and encrypted information for matching, ensuring privacy at all times.
   8. The solution shall enable FIU to be in full control of which data is used in such sharing processes.
We meet this requirement by allowing each FIU to determine exactly what data can be shared and under which conditions. The Pando application gives FIU granular control over data permissions, ensuring they have full autonomy over the use of their data in any sharing or matching processes.
   9. The solution shall enable FIU to share within limited groups of users. 
We meet this requirement by allowing each FIU to set specific data-sharing permissions that define which groups of users can access particular datasets. The Pando application includes configurable access control features, enabling FIU to limit data sharing within specific user groups.
   10. The solution shall enable FIU to facilitate follow-up processes to validate possible matches and initiate bilateral and/or multilateral information exchange using ESW.
We meet this requirement by allowing Pando to easily integrate with tools to facilitate the follow-up procedure.
   11. The solution shall limit the decision if and to what degree FIU use matching remains with the FIU only. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that each FIU has complete autonomy over whether and how they use the matching functionality, maintaining full control over their participation.
   12. The solution shall limit data transformation and matching are local processes. Only transformed data can leave the source. All non-transformed data remains at the source. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that all data transformations and matching computations are performed locally, with only the transformed results being shared externally.
   13. The solution should be built on a privacy-by-design approach. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that privacy is integrated at every stage of the system design, including data encryption, access control, and secure data sharing mechanisms.
   14. The solution must use the current technical framework, especially the security design and Identity and Access management elements. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring the Pando application can fully integrate with existing security infrastructure and IAM systems, allowing seamless compatibility and adherence to established security protocols.
   15. A decentralized approach to foster data security should be at least optional. 
We meet this requirement by providing the option for each FIU to run its own Pando instance independently, ensuring data is stored locally and reducing the risk of centralized data breaches.
   16. Automation should be supported for follow-up processes after a possible hit, fostering efficient processes for international collaboration. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring the Pando application can fully integrate automation features that support notifications, investigations, and collaboration tools to streamline international follow-up processes.
   6. Timeline
   1. January 2025: An overview of all required documents, including high-level planning and scope, will be delivered.
   2. March 2025: Detailed documents, including the IT Business Requirements Plan and a preliminary implementation plan, will be submitted. This will ensure thorough preparation for the HoFIU approval process in July 2025.
   3. April - June 2025: Review and finalization of detailed plans in coordination with EG and FIU stakeholders to address any feedback.
   4. July 2025: Presentation to Heads of Financial Intelligence Units (HoFIU) for endorsement.
   5. July 2025 - December 2025: Development phase, which includes the following:
   1. Development of add-on Pando features such as encrypted storage and search.
